name: Websites
summary: Accessible, maintainable business websites built around clear ownership, useful content, and the smallest architecture that fits.
problems: An existing website is dated, hard to maintain, slow, inaccessible, or unclear.
The business needs a new site without becoming dependent on an unnecessary platform.
Domain, hosting, source, deployment, or recovery ownership is unclear.
work: Discovery around audience, journeys, content, ownership, integrations, and constraints
Existing-site modernization before full rebuild when that is the better option
Responsive, accessible, performance-conscious implementation
Repository, hosting, deployment, handoff, and rollback documentation
ownership: Production accounts should remain customer-owned where practical, with LDW using named, scoped access.

faqs.question: Do I always need a complete website rebuild?
faqs.answer: No. LDW starts by understanding the current site, audience, content, ownership, integrations, and constraints. Modernizing what already works can be a better choice than replacing everything.

faqs.question: Who should own the domain, hosting, repository, and production accounts?
faqs.answer: The customer should ordinarily own production assets where practical, with LDW using named, scoped access. That keeps recovery, portability, and future handoff clearer.

faqs.question: Do you require a CMS or a specific website platform?
faqs.answer: No. The platform should fit the editing needs, integrations, support burden, portability, and budget. A static site, an existing platform, or a maintained service can each be the right answer in different situations.

proofNote: LDW uses the same delivery controls on its own production changes—reviewable source, protected-main review, automated browser/accessibility checks, documented rollback, and explicit ownership. That operating discipline is evidence of the method, not a client case study.

outcomes.title: A clearer first impression
outcomes.description: Organize the site around what visitors need to understand and do, instead of forcing them through an inherited page structure.

outcomes.title: A site the business can own
outcomes.description: Keep the domain, source, hosting and recovery model understandable, with customer-owned production assets where practical.

outcomes.title: A faster, more accessible experience
outcomes.description: Treat responsive behavior, accessibility and performance as delivery quality rather than optional cleanup after launch.

outcomes.title: A maintainable operating model
outcomes.description: Use the smallest architecture that fits the editing and integration needs, with documented deployment, rollback and handoff.

name: Website Care
summary: Bounded ongoing maintenance and improvement for websites that need a responsible technical owner without an unnecessary platform bundle.
problems: Updates and small fixes are handled reactively or not at all.
Accessibility, performance, dependencies, links, or content quality need periodic attention.
The business wants continuity after a project without giving up ownership.
work: Planned fixes and incremental improvements
Dependency and security upkeep within the agreed platform boundary
Accessibility, performance, link, and content-quality checks
Documented change history and owner-approved consequential changes
ownership: Website Care does not create a 24x7 support promise or transfer ownership of customer accounts to LDW.

faqs.question: Is Website Care a 24/7 emergency support plan?
faqs.answer: No. Website Care is bounded ongoing maintenance and improvement under an agreed support scope. It does not imply a 24/7 response commitment unless a separate agreement explicitly says so.

faqs.question: Does ongoing care mean LDW takes ownership of my website accounts?
faqs.answer: No. Ongoing support should preserve customer ownership. LDW generally works through named, scoped access rather than becoming the permanent recovery owner.

faqs.question: What kinds of work can Website Care include?
faqs.answer: Depending on the agreed scope, it can include planned fixes, dependency and security upkeep, accessibility and performance checks, link/content-quality review, and incremental improvements.

proofNote: LDW uses deterministic website-quality evidence and project-local browser/accessibility checks to inform human review. Scanner findings and scores are evidence, not automatic policy or ranking guarantees.

outcomes.title: A healthier site over time
outcomes.description: Handle planned fixes, upkeep, and incremental improvements before small problems become neglected technical debt.

outcomes.title: Clear ownership stays intact
outcomes.description: Keep the business in control of its accounts and source while LDW works through agreed, scoped access.

outcomes.title: Evidence for what needs attention
outcomes.description: Use accessibility, performance, dependency, link, and content checks to inform human review rather than chasing scores for their own sake.

name: Business Systems & Automation
summary: Configure and integrate existing systems first, then add automation or focused custom tooling only when a real operational gap remains.
problems: Staff repeat the same manual handoff or data-entry work.
Forms, files, email, CRM, scheduling, or other systems do not connect cleanly.
An existing tool nearly solves the problem but leaves a specific operational gap.
work: Workflow discovery and current-system inventory
Build-vs-buy and native-capability review before custom engineering
API, webhook, automation, and maintained-platform integration
Focused internal applications only when a measured gap remains
ownership: Automations should point back to authoritative systems rather than becoming a competing source of truth.

faqs.question: Do you start by building custom software?
faqs.answer: No. LDW first checks whether an existing platform, maintained service, native feature, API, webhook, or configuration change can solve the problem. Custom tooling is reserved for a real gap that remains.

faqs.question: Can you connect tools we already use?
faqs.answer: Often, yes. A typical engagement starts with workflow discovery and an inventory of the current systems, then looks for supported APIs, webhooks, automation paths, and maintained integrations.

faqs.question: Will the automation become another system we have to maintain as the source of truth?
faqs.answer: It should not. LDW prefers automations that move or transform information around authoritative systems rather than creating a competing source of truth.

proofNote: Document Control and Secure Exchange show how LDW explores real workflow gaps with synthetic/test-only evidence before claiming production maturity or provisioning customer infrastructure.

outcomes.title: Less repetitive manual work
outcomes.description: Reduce avoidable copying, re-entry, handoffs, and routine steps where supported automation can do the work reliably.

outcomes.title: Existing tools work together better
outcomes.description: Use native capabilities, APIs, webhooks, and maintained integrations before adding another application.

outcomes.title: A maintainable operating boundary
outcomes.description: Keep authoritative systems authoritative and make the automation understandable enough to support, change, or remove later.

name: Digital Ownership & Platform Administration
summary: Clarify who owns critical digital assets, who has access, how recovery works, and who is responsible for ongoing administration.
problems: Nobody is certain who owns the domain, DNS, hosting, repository, or business profile.
Former employees or vendors may still have access.
A provider transition or account cleanup needs to happen without breaking production systems.
work: Digital estate and account inventory
Customer-owned account and scoped-access planning
Vendor transition, offboarding, and recovery documentation
Ongoing administration where a clear recurring responsibility is agreed
ownership: LDW does not need to become the permanent recovery owner or collect master passwords when delegated access is available.
guideLabel: Read the website ownership & handoff guide

faqs.question: Can you help if we are not sure who owns our domain, DNS, hosting, repository, or business profiles?
faqs.answer: Yes. The work can start with a digital-estate inventory that identifies the current owner, access model, recovery path, and any transition or cleanup that is actually needed.

faqs.question: Do you need our master passwords or MFA recovery codes?
faqs.answer: No. Named users, delegated access, scoped roles, and customer-owned accounts are preferred. LDW should not become the permanent holder of master credentials or recovery secrets when safer access models exist.

faqs.question: Can you help move away from a former vendor or employee account?
faqs.answer: Yes, when the organization has authority to do so. The transition should document current state, proposed ownership, access changes, validation, and rollback so production systems are not broken during cleanup.

proofNote: The same ownership model is used internally: source, DNS, deployment, recovery, and administrative access are treated as explicit business assets rather than hidden vendor dependencies.

outcomes.title: A clear picture of what the business owns
outcomes.description: Identify the important accounts, assets, providers, recovery paths, and current access model.

outcomes.title: Safer access and transitions
outcomes.description: Use named or delegated access where possible and document vendor, employee, or administrator changes before making consequential moves.

outcomes.title: A recoverable operating model
outcomes.description: Leave ownership, recovery, handoff, and ongoing administrative responsibility understandable to the business.

name: Technology Consulting
summary: Practical architecture, troubleshooting, platform selection, and technical planning when the next step is not obvious.
problems: Several tools could solve the problem and the tradeoffs are unclear.
A technical issue needs root-cause review before more software is purchased.
The business needs a realistic roadmap rather than a large transformation program.
work: Architecture and platform-choice review
Troubleshooting and root-cause analysis
Cost, support, security, portability, and maintainability tradeoffs
A bounded roadmap with clear next actions
ownership: Consulting should leave the customer with clearer decisions and documentation, not a dependency on hidden provider knowledge.

faqs.question: Do I need a technical specification before we talk?
faqs.answer: No. A useful starting point is the business problem, what is happening today, the desired outcome, and the constraints that already matter.

faqs.question: Will consulting always lead to a build project?
faqs.answer: No. The result may be a configuration change, a platform decision, a troubleshooting finding, a small roadmap, or a recommendation to use an existing tool rather than build something new.

faqs.question: Can this be a small, focused engagement?
faqs.answer: Yes. LDW prefers bounded work that leaves the customer with clearer decisions, documentation, and next actions rather than expanding the scope without a demonstrated need.

proofNote: Consulting decisions can end in a roadmap, platform choice, configuration change, proof, or a recommendation not to build. The selected Work pages show those boundaries in practice.

outcomes.title: A clearer decision
outcomes.description: Turn competing options and technical uncertainty into documented tradeoffs and a practical recommendation or next step.

outcomes.title: A proportionate plan
outcomes.description: Match architecture, cost, support, security, and portability to the real need instead of defaulting to a large transformation.

outcomes.title: Permission not to build
outcomes.description: A useful outcome can be a configuration change, troubleshooting finding, maintained service, or recommendation to leave a working system alone.
